implementation_notes: C# implements the pattern in the language: `event` declares a multicast delegate field that only the declaring type may invoke or reset, += and -= subscribe and unsubscribe, and ?.Invoke raises the event safely with no subscribers. The Observer interface disappears - any method or lambda with the delegate's signature is an observer - so the classic Subject/Observer classes are only needed when observers must also be ordinary objects with identity. Follow the conventions: void-returning delegate type, sender plus event-args parameters, past-tense name for something that happened.
pitfalls: A lambda subscribed with += cannot be unsubscribed: the compiler creates a new delegate each time. Store the handler in a variable or subscribe a method group.
Each subscription is a strong reference from the publisher to the subscriber; a subscriber that never uses -= (e.g. a long-lived service or a view) stays alive and keeps being called.
Handler exceptions propagate to the raiser and abort the remaining invocation list, so one faulty subscriber can break the publisher's state change.
Events are not safe against concurrent subscription changes; raise a local copy (?.Invoke does) and synchronise subscription if it can happen on several threads.

variants.name: IObservable<T>/IObserver<T> (push-based notification contract)
variants.idiom_name: IObservable<T>.Subscribe returning IDisposable + Subject<T> from Rx.NET
variants.implementation_notes: The BCL defines push-based notification as a pair of interfaces: IObservable<T>.Subscribe(IObserver<T>) returns IDisposable, and the observer implements OnNext/OnError/OnCompleted, which makes unsubscribe a Dispose and gives the stream an explicit end-of-sequence and error channel. Rx.NET's Subject<T> is the publisher-side implementation and LINQ-style operators compose, filter and schedule the stream. Prefer it over the event keyword when the notifications form a stream that needs transformation, throttling, completion semantics or cancellation - and when the official documentation's own observer-pattern example (Unsubscriber as IDisposable) fits better than a multicast delegate.
variants.code_sketch:
var prices = new Subject<decimal>();
IDisposable sub = prices
    .Where(p => p < 80m)
    .Subscribe(p => Console.WriteLine($"below limit: {p}"));  // IObserver.OnNext
prices.OnNext(77m);      // notify
sub.Dispose();           // unsubscribe
// prices.OnError(ex) / prices.OnCompleted() end the sequence for every subscriber
pitfalls: The IDisposable returned by Subscribe must be disposed or the observer and its pipeline stay subscribed for the process lifetime.

Subject<T> is hot and not thread-safe by default: concurrent OnNext calls need a synchronised or scheduled subject, and late subscribers miss earlier values (use ReplaySubject/BehaviorSubject when that matters).
OnError/OnCompleted terminate the stream for all subscribers: per-subscriber error handling has to be inside the pipeline, not around Subscribe.
